props.title: The Tall Guy

sections.content: The Tall Guy marks Richard Curtis's first screenplay and Emma Thompson's film debut, delivering a quirky British romantic comedy that skewers both London's theater scene and medical rom-coms. Jeff Goldblum plays Dexter King, an American actor stuck playing straight man to an insufferable comedy star (Rowan Atkinson essentially parodying himself) in a long-running West End show. The film cleverly satirizes theatrical productions, culminating in a hilarious musical adaptation of "The Elephant Man" that predates both The Producers (2005) and Springtime for Hitler (1967) in its gleeful bad taste.

sections.content: Director Mel Smith and Curtis craft a love letter to London's theatrical world while simultaneously mocking its pretensions. The film shares DNA with later backstage comedies like Waiting for Guffman (1996) and Noises Off (1992), but maintains a distinctly British sensibility in its humor. Goldblum and Thompson's chemistry crackles, especially in their famous destructive sex scene that predates similar sequences in Jerry Maguire (1996) and Mr. & Mrs. Smith (2005).

The film's satirical take on medical romance, with Thompson's no-nonsense nurse Kate Lemmon, cleverly subverts tropes that would later become rom-com staples in films like Doc Hollywood (1991) and Green Card (1990). The subplot involving the musical "Elephant!" provides some of British comedy's most absurdly memorable moments, featuring songs like "He's Packing His Trunk" and "He's Not Just a Big Gray Thing." sections.content: The Tall Guy helped establish the template for the British romantic comedy renaissance of the 1990s. Its success paved the way for Curtis's later hits like Four Weddings and a Funeral (1994) and Notting Hill (1999), while also influencing films like Bridget Jones's Diary (2001) and Love Actually (2003). The film's willingness to mix sophisticated wordplay with broad physical comedy became a hallmark of Curtis's style.
